My trading mainly based on spotting where noticeable buyers and sellers are.. all other tech stuff comes after.

Keep in mind position sizing must be relevant to your account size. My view is that if you open a micro account it should be at least $5.000, for trading mini lots it shouldn't be less than $20.000 and for standard lots $100k + if you want want to survive and possibly get somewhere in markets.

Whiteout, there are times I risk up-to 5% but I try to keep it around 2% for any one of my accounts.

Sometimes, I have 10 or 15 open trades running with any one account. Then some may ask how the heck I can keep it within 2-5% account risk ratio. No, I don't have zillion $ accounts. Once any one of my trades locked, means at least stop moved to be +spread then that trade is no longer included in my risk pool.

One day I'll try to put together an article about "Risk Management" if and when I get around to do it. Risk management is THE Holly Grail of trading.

This is one of the reasons understanding what is actually happening in patterns like flags in terms of the price action helps to assess the 'quality' of the pattern and the likelihood of it working out.

The most common mistake I see people make (not on here - just generally) is with regards H&S patterns, people see them in all shapes and sizes without regard of the location relative to other TF's and to the market generally - let alone an understanding on what is actually occurring in an H&S pattern from a true price action perspective.

You've also highlighted the nuances off going from a relatively quiet session (Asia) to Frankfurt / London open - it's easy to see Asian low liquidity and thus tight consolidation as a flag or other pattern, taking care when you are approaching such a big jump in volume is always prudent IMO.

With regards flags specifically, another thing I would generally comment on is to remember what a flag is:

1. It's a continuation of a strong momentum move - it's a brief pause while price clears demand (for a short setup) and then moves on it's way. Thus it is logical that if the pole forms say over 2 hours and then price consolidates in the flag for 12 hours then the 'chances' of the flag working have somewhat decreased - because you're looking for that same momentum (which is a strong supply / demand imbalance) being present and price moving in the same vein it did when forming the pole.

2. The chances of a flag also working out if it retraces the whole pole distance are also decreased, why, because as a I said above a flag is a momentum continuation move so if price is retracing the whole move what does that tell us about the strength of the move that caused the pole - that supply / demand imbalance has been completely retraced.

Of course that latter could turn out to be compression back into the source of the pole for example, but then that's something different and not a flag.

I find when first understanding patterns if people (a) remember to think about what the pattern represents should be happening (b) understand the price action occurring within the pattern (c) remember to check the location and surrounding TF's and (d) check the market generally it helps to keep them out of trouble and focussing on identifying the more straight forward and obvious setups which helps to build confidence before moving onto more advanced concepts.

The name of this topic describes the understanding of price in its purest form.

When 2 people want to buy 1 available object, the object will go to the highest bid. Demand > Supply, price goes up.

When 2 people want to sell an identical object and there is 1 buyer who needs 1 object, the buyer will go for the lowest ask. Supply > Demand, price goes down.

When there is no supply or demand, there is no price.

When you look at a chart with price history(from any object), you will spot recent levels at which price reacted; A base/range where buyers and sellers agreed on price followed by an impulse. That impulse was triggered by a decision that caused supply and demand to go out of balance.

The level where this decision was made should be marked on your chart. There will be supply or demand left at that zone.

When buyers and sellers disagree on price, price will move to a previous level of agreement.

How price moves between levels is called Price Action(PA).

Since price is based on the opinions from buyers and sellers and not solely on facts, trading can't be science, therefor it must be an art. </nerdmode>

WRB: Wide Range Bodies = BIG CANDLES, lots of orders, heavy money making the price move fast and wild.

Hidden gaps: there is no space between the candles, so it is not a true gap. Hi Marc, What you are asking is really about the basics of supply and demand trading and it's important that you understand it. I wrote an article about Basic Supply & Demand some time ago, you can find it here: www.acegazette.com/en/trading-articles/s...s-levels-by-mel.html

This is important to know that price moves from Supply to Demand and from Demand to Supply. Why does price move from Demand to Supply? Simply because Buyers were in control at this particular point. Why does price move from Supply to Demand? Simply because Sellers were in control at this particular point.

Why is it that price can break Supply and become Demand? Simply because Buyers were in control at this particular point. Why is it that price can break Demand and become Supply? Simply because Sellers were in control at thos particular point.

Our edge is based on this simple facts. When price re-visit a Fresh Demand, we look to buy because there is a good chance that Big Money will have orders placed there and vice versa for a re-vist of a Fresh Supply.

I suspect that the "brief pause" you are reffering to is what we call a Base. You can find more info about it by clicking on the link to the article.

Now about the Swing high and low, imo, those are mostly just retests of a previous Supply & Demand areas...

1 thing that frustrates me is when entering a zone, does price react on the spikes or bodies of candles. To me they both seem to happen. So here is my latest logic.

Lets say my account is £10,000

My total risk on any one trade is 1%, that = £100, for me to risk in a zone

so in a marked box zone of 50 pips top to bottom

This allows me a lot size of £2 per pip. So if my trade fails i have only lost £100 or 1% of my account.

Now, if i have 1 limit order with the above equation, it allows me one chance to enter the market.

But if i break the lot size down to 0.50p per pip, i can have 4 limit orders at various areas in the zone. And still only risk 1%!

So when price enters my zone it could pick up some or all orders.

This allows me with metatrader to also take part profits on 1 or 2 of those micro orders, as price hits mid targets. If i have one order on IBFX, i can not part close 1 large order.

Sorry the explanation was long winded,hopefully you can see my full reasoning behind a method that suits my trading and my lifestyle.
